meta.subtitle: AWS grew 37% in Q2'26, its fastest in 18 quarters, while AI capex turned trailing free cash flow negative and the multiple stays full

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate Amazon BUY with a 12-month target range of $285 to $350, against a current price of $249.27. Amazon reported Q2'26 net sales of $200.6 billion, {+ up 20% +} year over year, and operating income of $27.5 billion, {+ up 43% +} year over year. AWS was the profit engine: segment operating income of $16.6 billion, up from $10.2 billion a year earlier, on segment sales that grew 37% — the press release calls it AWS's fastest growth in 18 quarters, to a $169 billion annualized run rate. North America operating income was $9.1 billion and International was $1.7 billion. The bullish reading is the durability of that AWS reacceleration plus 26% advertising growth; the bearish reading is that capital expenditure of $131.8 billion in FY25, which the company expects to increase in 2026, keeps free cash flow negative — trailing-twelve-month free cash flow was an outflow of $7.6 billion. At 20.1x trailing earnings and 16.2x EV/EBITDA the stock is not cheap, and the Street consensus target of $329.29 already prices in a lot; we set a base case below it. Our BUY rests on a positive probability-weighted expected upside of about 17.5%; with reward/risk near 0.99x the reward roughly balances the risk, so this is a constructive call rather than a bet that the multiple re-rates from here.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Amazon.com, Inc. was incorporated in 1994 and is headquartered in Seattle, Washington. It engages in the retail sale of consumer products, advertising, and subscription services through online and physical stores in North America and internationally. The company reports three segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). It manufactures and sells electronic devices such as Kindle, Echo, and Ring, and it develops and produces media content. It runs marketplace programs that let third-party sellers reach its customers, and it offers Amazon Prime, a membership program. AWS provides compute, storage, database, analytics, machine learning, and other services. In FY25 Amazon generated revenue of $716.9 billion, {+ up 12.4% +}, with net income of $77.7 billion and diluted EPS of $7.17. The most recent quarter, Q2'26 ended June 30, 2026, brought net sales of $200.6 billion, {+ up 20% +} year over year. The company carries a market capitalization near $2.69 trillion on roughly 10.79 billion shares and pays no dividend.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: Amazon is two businesses in one financial statement. A large, low-margin retail and marketplace operation funds AWS, a high-margin cloud franchise that supplies most of the profit. In Q2'26 AWS produced $16.6 billion of segment operating income out of $27.5 billion consolidated, on segment sales that grew 37% year over year. The investment case rests on AWS holding that growth as enterprises adopt AI, while advertising — up 26% year over year in Q2'26 — adds a second high-margin stream. Against this, Amazon is spending heavily: FY25 capital expenditure was $131.8 billion and management expects it to rise in 2026, which pushed trailing-twelve-month free cash flow to an outflow of $7.6 billion. At 20.1x trailing earnings the shares require the capital cycle to convert into durable AWS and advertising profit. We think it likely does, but the margin of safety is thin, so we rate the shares BUY rather than more.

catalysts: Sustained AWS reacceleration: the segment reached a $169 billion annualized run rate in Q2'26, and holding that pace is the main upside driver.

AI and chips scaling: each business passed a $25 billion annualized run rate with triple-digit percentage growth, with Trainium winning multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitments from Anthropic and OpenAI.
Advertising momentum: a high-margin advertising business that scales with retail and Prime Video traffic.
Near-term guidance: Q3'26 operating income of $22.5 billion to $26.5 billion, versus $17.4 billion a year earlier.
risks: The AI capital program keeps free cash flow negative on a trailing basis, and management expects capital spending to rise further in 2026 — the payback timeline is the central company-specific risk.
The valuation, at 16.2x EV/EBITDA, leaves little room for an AWS growth disappointment.
The company competes in intensely competitive markets across retail, cloud, advertising, and devices, per its own risk factors.
Headline earnings are flattered by a large one-time Anthropic-related gain, so reported EPS overstates Amazon's operating earnings power (detailed under risks).

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue has compounded steadily: $469.8 billion in FY21, $514.0 billion in FY22, $574.8 billion in FY23, $638.0 billion in FY24, and $716.9 billion in FY25, a {+ 12.4% +} FY25 increase. Gross margin has widened every year, from 42.0% in FY21 to 50.3% in FY25, as higher-margin AWS and advertising grew faster than retail. Operating income tells a sharper story of operating leverage: it fell to $12.2 billion in FY22, then recovered to $36.9 billion in FY23, $68.6 billion in FY24, and $80.0 billion in FY25, lifting operating margin from 2.4% to 11.2%. Net income swung from {- a net loss of $2.7 billion -} in FY22 to $77.7 billion in FY25, with diluted EPS of $7.17. The Q2'26 quarter continued the pattern on the operating line: net sales of $200.6 billion, up 20% year over year, and operating income of $27.5 billion, up 43%, for an operating margin of 13.7% (the snapshot rounds this to 14%). Reported net income was flattered by a large one-time non-operating gain, so the operating result — not the headline figure — is the cleaner read on the quarter.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Amazon's balance sheet is a source of strength. Cash and short-term investments rose to $123.0 billion at FY25 from $101.2 billion a year earlier, and the MD&A confirms cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities of $123.0 billion at both December 31, 2025 and June 30, 2026. Total debt was $68.9 billion at FY25, leaving net debt of -$18.0 billion — a {+ net cash position +}. Shareholders' equity has more than doubled over the period, from $138.2 billion in FY21 to $411.1 billion in FY25, retained through earnings rather than diluted away. On a trailing basis net debt to EBITDA is 0.3x and interest coverage is 28.1x, so leverage is not a concern even as the company funds a heavy capital program. The current ratio is modest at 1.05 for FY25 and 1.03 on a trailing basis, typical for a retailer that turns payables quickly. The company reported no borrowings outstanding under its revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs as of June 30, 2026, though it raised $82.4 billion of debt proceeds during the six months ended June 30, 2026 to help fund investment.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow is strong and growing: $139.5 billion in FY25, up from $115.9 billion in FY24, and the press release reports $161.4 billion on a trailing-twelve-month basis, {+ up 33% +} from $121.1 billion a year earlier. The problem for free-cash-flow investors is the capital line. Capital expenditure was $131.8 billion in FY25, up from $83.0 billion in FY24, and management expects it to increase again in 2026. As a result FY25 free cash flow was just $7.7 billion, an FCF margin of 1.1%, and on a trailing-twelve-month basis free cash flow swung to {- an outflow of $7.6 billion -}, which the press release attributes to a $66.1 billion year-over-year increase in property and equipment purchases for AI. Trailing FCF yield is {- -0.4% -}. Amazon is also deploying cash into AI equity stakes: cash capital expenditure was $53.1 billion in Q2'26, and the company invested $28.7 billion in OpenAI's Series C preferred stock over the six months ended June 30, 2026 (including $13.7 billion in Q2'26) plus $10.0 billion in Anthropic nonvoting preferred stock in Q2'26. No dividend is paid.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Amazon trades at 20.1x trailing earnings, 3.5x sales, and 16.2x EV/EBITDA, with a forward P/E of 19.4x on next-twelve-month estimates. On FY27 consensus EPS of $10.48 the forward multiple is about 23.8x; we anchor on FY27 rather than FY26 because the FY26 estimate is lifted by a one-time non-operating gain detailed under risks. None of these multiples is demanding for a business compounding revenue in the low-teens with expanding margins, but none is cheap either. The pack shows a company column only, with peers pending a peer data source, so there is no peer comparison to lean on; in any case, the retail-heavy names usually screened against Amazon miss its cloud and advertising economics, and we place no weight on peer multiples. The more useful anchor is Amazon's own cash generation and the AWS profit trajectory. The Street consensus target is $329.29, a median of $328.00, within a range of $230.00 to $405.00; the wide spread reflects genuine disagreement about how fast the AI capital cycle converts to profit.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: AWS sustains growth near the 37% posted in Q2'26 as AI adoption broadens, advertising holds its 26% year-over-year pace, and operating income tracks toward the high end of guidance; the market keeps paying a premium multiple.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue advances toward the FY26 consensus of $828.3 billion (+16%) and FY27 of $947.8 billion, AWS stays the profit engine and margins hold; free cash flow stays thin while capital spending remains elevated, so the multiple does not expand.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: AWS growth decelerates as AI demand normalizes or competition intensifies, capital expenditure above the FY25 level of $131.8 billion keeps free cash flow negative, and the multiple compresses toward the low end of the Street's $230.00 target.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The three scenarios weight to a fair value modestly below the Street. We assign the base case a 45% probability, the bear 33%, and the bull 22%, reflecting real uncertainty about how quickly the AI capital cycle converts to free cash flow. The base implied price of $315 sits below the Street's consensus target, and our 12-month target range of $285 to $350 brackets it. The bear case at $205 sits about 17.8% below the current price of $249.27 — a genuine downside, not a token — if AWS decelerates and capital spending stays elevated. The bull case at $380 stops short of the top of the Street's target range because the shares already discount a good deal of the AWS reacceleration. On these weights the probability-weighted expected upside is about 17.5%, a reward/risk near 0.99x, so the reward roughly balances the risk. The positive expected value supports a BUY, but the near-even reward/risk argues against a more aggressive stance while free cash flow is negative and the multiple is full.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor's data feed supplies no revenue split, so this pack carries one consolidated line, but Amazon reports three segments — North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) — and the Q2'26 press release breaks them out. AWS generated $16.6 billion of segment operating income, up from $10.2 billion a year earlier, on sales of $42.2 billion that grew 37% year over year, reaching a $169 billion annualized run rate. North America contributed $9.1 billion of operating income on sales of $116.2 billion, up 16%, and International contributed $1.7 billion of operating income on sales that grew 15%. The read-through is that a low-margin retail and marketplace base drives volume and customer relationships, while AWS supplies the bulk of the profit and is growing far faster than the retail segments. AWS's AI and chips businesses each passed a $25 billion annualized run rate with triple-digit percentage growth, and Graviton is used by 98% of the top 1,000 EC2 customers.

moatFactors.name: Cost advantage and scale
moatFactors.body: Amazon's fulfillment network, purchasing scale, and custom silicon lower unit costs below what smaller rivals can match. Gross margin has climbed from 42.0% in FY21 to 50.3% in FY25 as scale and mix improved. Graviton's broad adoption across AWS's top EC2 customers is evidence that its price-performance advantage is entrenched.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs (AWS)
moatFactors.body: Enterprises that build on AWS compute, storage, database, and machine-learning services face high migration costs, which shows up in a large and rapidly growing revenue run rate. Multi-year, multi-gigawatt Trainium commitments from Anthropic and OpenAI lengthen those lock-ins.

moatFactors.name: Network effects (marketplace)
moatFactors.body: Amazon's marketplace pairs a large buyer base with third-party sellers; more sellers widen selection, which draws more buyers, and Prime membership reinforces the loop. This flywheel underpins the scale of the North America retail segment.

moatFactors.name: Brand and advertising intangibles
moatFactors.body: The Amazon brand and its shopper data power an advertising business that grew 26% year over year in Q2'26, an industry-typically high-margin stream layered on retail and Prime Video traffic.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is durable but not unassailable. AWS's switching costs and Amazon's cost scale are hard to replicate, and the AI capital cycle — $131.8 billion of FY25 capital expenditure, rising in 2026 — is widening the gap in cloud infrastructure. The risk is that the competitive intensity Amazon flags in its risk factors, from hyperscale cloud rivals and well-funded new entrants, compresses returns before the current investment pays off. The advertising and AWS profit streams give the business pricing power that pure retailers lack, which is why we rate the moat wide, but the durability of returns depends on the capital program converting to free cash flow rather than perpetually consuming it.

points: AWS is the primary profit lever. Cloud migration and AI training workloads drive demand, and enterprise commitments renew over multiple years, which makes the $169 billion annualized run rate defensible rather than one-off. The counter-case is that this is also the swing factor: if AI training demand normalizes or hyperscaler price competition intensifies, the segment that supplies most of the profit slows, so the quarterly AWS growth rate is the number to watch.

Custom silicon is the mechanism behind AWS's cost position and lock-in. Trainium and the chips business, each past a $25 billion run rate, let Amazon serve AI workloads more cheaply than merchant-GPU rivals, and multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitments from Anthropic and OpenAI extend the backlog. The risk is execution: those commitments depend on the capital program delivering data-center capacity on time.

Advertising is a second high-margin engine typical of the industry. It monetizes existing shopper and Prime Video traffic at low incremental cost, so its 26% year-over-year growth in Q2'26 adds operating leverage. What to watch is whether that pace holds as ad load matures and as privacy and regulatory pressure on targeting builds.

Retail volume growth is slower but funds the flywheel. North America sales rose 16% and International 15% in Q2'26 while Amazon added Prime members, faster delivery, and grocery density that deepen the customer relationships AWS and advertising then monetize. The risk is that retail margins stay thin and consumer demand softens in a downturn.

Near-term, Q3'26 guidance frames the trajectory: operating income of $22.5 billion to $26.5 billion versus $17.4 billion a year earlier, though the top-line range of $197.0 billion to $202.0 billion implies growth decelerating to between 9% and 12% as Prime Day timing and foreign-exchange headwinds weigh.

management.leadership: Andy Jassy is President and CEO. On the Q2'26 results he described AWS as 'booming, growing 36.7% year-over-year in Q2,' and noted the AI and chips businesses each eclipsed run rates of more than $25 billion. The leadership record is one of long-horizon investment: Amazon's heavy reinvestment, rising further in 2026, is consistent with its history of spending ahead of demand, first in fulfillment and now in AI infrastructure. The counter-case is that this style tolerates years of negative free cash flow, and shareholders must trust that the investments earn their cost of capital.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is dominated by reinvestment. FY25 capital expenditure was $131.8 billion, up from $83.0 billion in FY24, and it is set to rise again in 2026, which is why free cash flow is thin to negative despite $161.4 billion of trailing operating cash flow. Amazon pays no dividend and has not repurchased stock in recent years. It is also making sizable AI equity investments: $28.7 billion into OpenAI's Series C over the six months ended June 30, 2026 (with $21.3 billion of remaining commitment funded after quarter-end) and $10.0 billion into Anthropic nonvoting preferred stock in Q2'26. The balance sheet — net debt of -$18.0 billion and 0.3x net debt to EBITDA — gives management room to keep investing, but the discipline question is whether these outlays clear their return hurdle.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A filed April 9, 2026. On independence, the proxy names Gen. Alexander, Ms. Cooper, Ms. Gorelick, Dr. Huttenlocher, Dr. Ng, Mrs. Nooyi, Mr. Rubinstein, Mr. Smith, Ms. Stonesifer, and Mr. Weeks as independent under Nasdaq rules; the captured excerpt does not give the total board size, so we note the named independents rather than infer a majority. It discloses only immaterial ordinary-course payments to Corning (Mr. Weeks) and DeepLearning.AI (Dr. Ng). Risk oversight is delegated to Audit, Leadership Development and Compensation, Nominating and Corporate Governance, and Security committees. Executive pay is anchored on long-vesting restricted stock units with base salaries set deliberately below peers; Mr. Jassy has received no equity grant since 2021, so his pay moves with the stock. Say-on-pay drew 78% support at the 2025 annual meeting — a solid but not overwhelming endorsement worth monitoring.

idiosyncratic: Free cash flow is negative on a trailing basis: an outflow of $7.6 billion for the twelve months ended June 30, 2026, driven by a $66.1 billion year-over-year jump in property and equipment purchases for AI. FY25 free cash flow was only $7.7 billion (a 1.1% margin), and with capital expenditure of $131.8 billion set to rise in 2026, the payback on AI infrastructure is the central company-specific risk.

Reported earnings quality is uneven. Q2'26 net income of $62.6 billion included $53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income, primarily from the Anthropic investment; that one-time gain is also why FY26 consensus EPS of $12.88 sits above FY27's $10.48. Excluding it, headline profitability overstates the operating run rate that the quarter's operating result captures more faithfully.

AWS growth is the swing factor. It grew 37% in Q2'26, and a normalization of AI demand or a share shift to competing hyperscalers would hit the segment that supplied $16.6 billion of Q2'26 operating income — most of the consolidated total — and therefore most of Amazon's profit growth.
Inventory and supplier-commitment risk: management notes that each additional 1% of inventory valuation allowance as of June 30, 2026 would add roughly $405 million to cost of sales.
risks.systemic: Amazon is exposed to the macro cycle on both sides of its model. Its own risk factors flag fluctuations in foreign exchange rates and energy prices, global economic conditions, tariff and trade policies, interest rates, and supply volatility including for memory chips. Consumer demand drives the retail and advertising businesses, and enterprise IT budgets drive AWS, so a recession would pressure both. As a large multinational, Amazon also carries international risks — local regulation, trade and tariff measures, currency restrictions, and geopolitical events — that it details in its filings. Q3'26 guidance already assumes an unfavorable foreign-exchange impact of about 80 basis points. None of these is unique to Amazon, but the company's scale makes it sensitive to all of them at once.

body: Our recommendation is BUY, with a 12-month target range of $285 to $350. The case is straightforward: AWS is reaccelerating — 37% growth in Q2'26 to a $169 billion run rate — and advertising is compounding at 26%, together lifting operating income to $27.5 billion in the quarter, up 43% year over year. Those two high-margin engines, funded by a low-margin retail base, justify a premium multiple and support upside toward our base case of $315, modestly below the Street's $329.29 consensus.

The reason we stop at BUY rather than a stronger call is the cash-flow and valuation setup. FY25 capital expenditure of $131.8 billion is rising in 2026, trailing free cash flow is an outflow of $7.6 billion, and at 20.1x trailing earnings the shares leave little room for an AWS disappointment. Our bear case of $205 — about 17.8% below the current $249.27 — is a real risk, not a formality, if the AI capital cycle fails to convert to free cash flow on schedule.

Net, the reward roughly balances the risk — reward/risk near 0.99x on a positive expected value — which supports a BUY rather than a stronger call. We would own Amazon for the AWS and advertising profit trajectory and the balance-sheet strength (net cash, 0.3x net debt to EBITDA), while watching the capital program and free cash flow closely as the signal on whether the current investment earns its return.
